title: Where Muslims differ
hook: some embrace orders and saints' shrines, others hold these as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nafs: the self that commands, the self that blames, the self at peace. Your line was train the self. Which one spoke loudest? Day three hundred seven.

Picture two Muslim families on the same Friday. The first drives out after the prayer to a saint's tomb, a white dome with green cloth over the grave. They recite al-Fatiha for him, ask God for help near the resting place of a man they love, and give food to the poor at the gate. The second family, just as devout, would never go. They'd say, with conviction, that this isn't how the Prophet and his companions practiced, and that prayer should be directed to God alone, with nothing that looks like a go-between. For two weeks we've walked the Sufi path. Today, honestly, where Muslims differ.
screen: `A WHITE DOME, A GREEN CLOTH.` → `A FAMILY THAT WOULD NEVER GO.` → `BOTH DEVOUT.`

segments.voice: For most of Islamic history, Sufism was part of the mainstream. Great scholars of law, like al-Ghazali, were Sufis. Across the Ottoman lands, South Asia, West Africa and Southeast Asia, many ordinary Muslims belonged to an order, and visiting the shrines of saints was common. Many Muslims today still hold to that. Other Muslims have long criticized parts of it. The scholar Ibn Taymiyyah, in the fourteenth century, respected early Sufis like Junayd, but he condemned practices at graves that he believed compromised tawhid, the oneness of God. Modern Salafi movements, which aim to follow the salaf, the first generations of Muslims, hold that orders, shrine visits and musical sama' are later additions, bid'ah, and some reject tasawwuf as a separate path altogether. And many Muslims stand in between: they value tasawwuf as purifying the heart, and question some practices. Shia Muslims, for their part, visit the shrines of the Prophet's family, and their relation to the Sufi orders varies. These are real differences, and sometimes painful ones. But notice what every side says. Each argues from the Qur'an and the sunnah. The Qur'an itself tells believers, when they dispute, in Pickthall's words, to "refer it to Allah and the messenger." And a hadith in al-Bukhari says that a scholar who does his best to reach a ruling and gets it right has two rewards, and one who does his best and gets it wrong still has one. Disagreement, in Arabic ikhtilaf, is old in Islam. Underneath it, the same Book.
screen: `FOR CENTURIES, PART OF THE MAINSTREAM.` · `IBN TAYMIYYAH AND THE SALAFI CRITIQUE.` · `MANY STAND IN BETWEEN.` · `REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.` · then, large: `THE SAME QUR'AN UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two views at once, respectfully. Sit, and breathe. Picture the two families from the hook. Imagine sitting with the first at the shrine, and understanding why it moves them. Then imagine sitting with the second, and understanding why it worries them. You don't have to decide. Just hold both, with respect, for a few breaths. Then bring it closer: think of someone in your own family you disagree with, and try the same. If you pray, you can pray for both. The bell holds the time.
Where Muslims differ. On orders, shrines and music, Muslims disagree, and all of them argue from the same Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: the same qur'an underneath. Today, in one disagreement, name out loud what you and the other person share before you name what you don't. Day three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Muslims differ on Sufi orders, visiting saints' shrines and music in worship: many embrace them, Salafi Muslims and others reject them as later additions, and many take a middle position, while all appeal to the Qur'an and the sunnah.

what a scholar hears: Ibn Taymiyyah's critique of ziyarah practices, modern Salafi reform, and the hadith of the two rewards for ijtihad (al-Bukhari 7352).
